title: World from Motion: Generative Dynamic Gaussian Reconstruction from Monocular Video
claim: Starting from a flawed, incomplete reconstruction, a generative model's outputs are distilled into a refined, complete representation with better motion.
layout: Left 4-column by 3-row image grid, right 2 stacked panels; progression arrow
description: The left side is a grid of real video frames with four columns: Input Monocular Video, Initial Dynamic 3DGS, Multi-view Video Samples, and Refined Dynamic 3DGS. The three rows are timesteps t=20, 60 and 100, and each shows a person carrying a box past a piano in a store. The initial 3DGS column has large white holes and smeared, blurry geometry. The multi-view samples and refined columns are complete and sharp from new viewpoints. A grey arrow under the grid reads 'Progression of World from Motion'. A vertical divider separates the grid from the right side. The right side has two stacked panels, Initial vs Refined Dynamic 3DGS, which overlay colored motion trajectories on a person in a multi-exposure view. The refined version has cleaner, more coherent trajectories. The eye goes first to the left grid and its contrast between the white-hole column and the clean columns.
caption: \textbf{\method{} reconstructs a dynamic 3DGS world from the camera and scene motion in a single monocular video.} From an input video and an initial reconstruction produced by MoSca [ref], our video model generates novel views that are distilled into a refined reconstruction. Our method faithfully recovers observed structure and synthesizes plausible novel-view dynamics, in turn improving the underlying scene motion, as visualized on the right.
abstract: We present World from Motion, a method for generating freely renderable dynamic 3D Gaussian representations from monocular videos. Our approach conditions a video model on dense, pixel-aligned renderings that encode appearance, geometry, and 3D scene motion along both input and target camera trajectories to correct rendering artifacts and fill in missing regions from an initial reconstruction. To train this model, we construct a dataset of aligned multiview video pairs and dynamic 3DGS representations, with simulated artifacts characteristic of monocular reconstruction. At test time, we distill the model's generations, including newly observed regions and motions, back into a single consistent, high-quality dynamic 3DGS, improving both novel-view synthesis and the underlying 3D motion. Our method sets a new state of the art in 4D reconstruction and seamlessly generalizes to in-the-wild videos with large viewpoint changes and dynamic motions.
